overview: East Germany was the German Democratic Republic (GDR), founded in 1949 in the Soviet occupation zone. The SED controlled politics and travel; families also worked, learned, played and made homes under these constraints. Women’s jobs and childcare were more common than in West Germany, but housework remained unequal. Prefab flats, holiday camps and school clubs belong alongside the Wall, surveillance and protest in this history. Peaceful revolution and a free vote in 1990 led to the GDR joining the Federal Republic on 3 October. The imported map shows it from 1960 to 1994, which is not its real lifespan.

periods.title: Founding and rebuilding
periods.summary: The SED dominated the new state; families faced postwar shortages as industry, housing and childcare were organized under socialism.

periods.title: Wall and socialist constitution
periods.summary: The 1961 Wall restricted movement; the 1968 constitution openly entrenched SED leadership.

periods.title: Prefab homes and managed daily life
periods.summary: Mass apartments and childcare expanded, while shortages, travel restrictions and the party’s political control remained.

periods.title: Peaceful revolution and unification
periods.summary: Protests and the Wall’s opening led to a free Volkskammer election and accession to the Federal Republic.

items.text: The GDR was founded on 7 October 1949. The imported border data begins in 1960 and lasts to 1994, but the separate East German state actually ended in 1990. A polygon’s available years are not a state’s biography.
Before 1990, the Volkskammer looked like a parliament but its seat allocations kept SED control secure. Ordinary voters lacked a free choice among competing governing parties.

On 13 August 1961 the GDR sealed the Berlin border and built the Wall. A grandmother, parent or friend across town could suddenly become much harder to visit; the barrier was a family event as well as a Cold War symbol.

An original German phrase in the 1968 constitution called the GDR a “sozialistischer Staat deutscher Nation,” meaning a “socialist state of the German nation.” It stated the regime’s self-description; the same constitution entrenched SED leadership.
After demonstrations in 1989 and the Wall’s opening, East Germans voted freely for the Volkskammer in March 1990. That vote helped decide the state’s future.

Many women worked for pay, and the state promised nursery care and support for mothers. Yet women often earned less and still did much of the cooking, cleaning and child care. Equality on a poster did not automatically wash the dishes.

A child’s first school day might feature a Schultüte, a cone filled with treats and supplies. Young Pioneers mixed after-school activities with the state’s political education, so school had both familiar childhood rituals and ideology.

Summer could mean a state-organized holiday camp with swimming, hikes, crafts or sport. Some children camped with family instead; the Federal Archives records several kinds of holiday, not one universal childhood.
The reconstructed 1980s GDR living room in the DDR Museum is a reminder that people ate, watched television, played games and celebrated birthdays inside a state that also policed politics.

Postwar apartment shortages led the state to allocate housing and build prefabricated Plattenbau neighborhoods. New flats could put a school, shop and kindergarten nearby, while older buildings often waited for repairs.

In a prized 1970s or 1980s prefab flat, the tiny bathroom might fit a bathtub, toilet and hot-water tap. In an older building, a private bathroom might still be a dream. “Nasszelle,” or “wet cell,” was a rather honest name for that compact room.

The DDR Museum describes state-covered visits to doctors and children’s checkups, but also long waits and medicine shortages. The record of eastern facilities at unification shows why access and quality are different questions.

Neighbors in a prefab building could organize celebrations together; some enjoyed that closeness, while others disliked the pressure of being watched. A block of flats was a real community, not simply a gray shape on the map.

ending.text: The GDR ceased to be a separate state on 3 October 1990 when it joined the continuing Federal Republic. Its last free parliament had been elected in March. People, homes and memories endured; the imported 1994 border endpoint is a data artifact, not a later political ending.
